posts.title: Financing primary care after the donors leave
posts.excerpt: The post-donor transition is treated as a budgeting exercise. It is really a question about who holds the risk when the external money stops.
posts.body:
The post-donor transition is treated as a budgeting exercise. It is really a question about who holds the risk when the external money stops — and most systems have never asked it out loud.

This is sample content. Log in at /admin to replace it with the full essay.

posts.excerpt: Every team has the person who absorbs the chaos. The trouble is that their heroism is also why the chaos never gets fixed.

posts.title: Models don't have judgment. Systems do.
posts.excerpt: The interesting question was never whether the model is accurate. It's what the clinic does with a number it half-trusts at 2am.

posts.title: The continuum of care is a promise, not a diagram
posts.excerpt: We draw it as a clean line from pregnancy to old age. Patients experience it as a series of cliffs.

posts.excerpt: Good policy fails when it's treated as a design problem instead of what it actually is: a question of who you can keep on side.

posts.title: What a clinic actually wants from an algorithm
posts.excerpt: Not accuracy. Not explainability. It wants to not be blamed when it follows the recommendation and the patient still dies.

posts.excerpt: Universal coverage is a budget line that nobody wants to own. Until that changes, the rest is rhetoric.

posts.title: Before equity, Before Liberty
posts.body:
**Before Liberty. Before Equity.**

*Enablement as the Foundation of Human Agency* 

Yonas Hagos



## **I. The *Distance***  

There is something that surfaces in almost every honest conversation I have had. Something every person, once the pretence falls away, appears to want.  Not just survival, but a palatable and meaningful existence. To love and be loved. To belong somewhere. To move through life with enough dignity to feel that it is, on balance, worth living. This may sound naive to the hardened observer and obvious to the idealist. But strip away the politics, the frameworks, the funding cycles, and what remains, at the irreducible centre of it all, is this:

***Every human being is trying to avoid suffering they did not choose.***

And of all the forces that shape whether a person suffers or flourishes, few present themselves as urgently, as visibly, as personally as health. Sickness does not wait for convenient timing. It arrives uninvited into the middle of a life — into the love, the belonging, the dignity — and rearranges everything. It is perhaps why, of all human concerns, health has attracted the most organised, most sustained, most globally coordinated response. Nothing positions itself more consistently at the intersection of suffering and hope than the healthcare system.

That distance, between the life people want and the life structural reality permits, is written most legibly in one's wellbeing. One sees it in the patient who walks three hours to a clinic that may or may not have what she needs. In the community health worker, navigating systems designed without him in mind. In the mother rationing medication because the month is longer than the prescription. In the child who is bright and hungry and being failed by both conditions simultaneously.

And then one looks up, at the systems built supposedly for these same people.

Governments ration health. They position themselves as protectors of their citizens' wellbeing, partly out of genuine duty, partly out of something more transactional.  A healthy population is a productive population. A productive population is a mobilisable one. The citizen’s health and the state’s interest overlap, but they are not the same thing. Philanthropies and NGOs move in every direction with genuine intention. Frameworks multiply. Conferences convene. Declarations are signed.

And all of it is measured in output. One of those measurements is the DALY, the Disability-Adjusted Life Year—a life year, adjusted for disability. When one sits with that definition honestly, it reveals what is really being optimised for: the reduction of incapacitated human capacity.

Not flourishing. Not potential. Capacity. Quantified. Adjusted. Managed.

**And yet the wall remains.**

Despite the effort, the investment, the genuine sacrifice of people who have given careers and sometimes lives to this work, the safe haven stays out of reach. The gap between what health systems deliver and what human beings actually need persists with a stubbornness that demands explanation. Something structural is missing. Not in the commitment of the people inside these systems. In the logic of the systems themselves.

One imagines a different world. Perhaps a utopia, or perhaps simply the honest ambition of what health systems were always meant to be.  A world where individuals finally attain their own vision of health. Where governments, NGOs, and philanthropies take a breath, receive their certificate of completion, and assume their rightful seat, not as providers, but as guardians of a fair state they helped build.  Observers. Structuralists. Custodians of something that no longer requires emergency intervention.

We are not there. 

Cognisant of the great strides made, in child mortality, in vaccine coverage, in the expansion of primary care, the honest observer must acknowledge the distance covered and the distance that remains. And in every serious conversation about closing that gap, one concept surfaces with the consistency of a north star. Proposed, debated, funded, measured, and invoked as the engine that will close the distance.

***Equity.***

It appears in every boardroom, every policy document, every funding proposal, a full stop at the end of every sentence. Invoked to attract funders, signal alignment, nod that yes: we are all moving in the same direction, aboard the equity-branded wagon. Yet one might pause and ask the question that tends to make rooms uncomfortable:

***Would the equity-branded wagon actually take us there — or does it first need a road that has not yet been built?***

It is in sitting with that question that one encounters Richard Horton’s 2018 provocation in The Lancet, and finds oneself in a conversation that is difficult to leave.

## **II. Liberty First: A Compelling Provocation**

[Horton’s argument](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(18)30724-4/fulltext) is worth taking seriously, not as provocation for its own sake, but because it names something real that equity language often conceals. He argues that equity cannot be global health’s defining objective. Not because fairness is unimportant. But because equity, as a framework, is largely silent on power. It describes a destination without interrogating who controls the road. And in that silence, the forces that produce inequity — authoritarian governance, extractive markets, structural exclusion — remain comfortably unchallenged.

His answer is liberty — and behind it, dignity. The sovereign right of every person to be an end in themselves, not a means to someone else’s agenda. Ill-health, in this framing, is not merely suffering. It is a restriction of freedom. The person who cannot breathe well cannot think fully. The child stunted by malnutrition cannot reach the cognitive potential that education assumes she has. Health and liberty are, on this point, deeply and inseparably connected.

He is not wrong. And this is where most critics of his argument make their mistake — dismissing it before sitting with what it genuinely illuminates.

But before following Horton to liberty, something else requires naming. Most equity initiatives share an unspoken grammar of care:

***We have chosen to care. We will capacitate the vulnerable. We will represent those who cannot represent themselves.***

The intention is genuine. But one might notice what this grammar quietly encodes. The capacity, the agency, the voice — it remains with the helper. The vulnerable remain the object of the intervention. Not its subject. Not its author. The helper, in other words, needs the helped to remain helpable.

And so the question arises — one that rarely appears in strategy documents: when exactly does the vulnerable graduate? At what point is the document signed that says you now have full agency, and we are no longer needed? When does the equity initiative design for its own irrelevance?

That moment is almost never built into the architecture. Institutions are rarely incentivised to dismantle the mandate that justifies their existence. And this reveals something structural: if equity is a fairness maximisation engine — transferring power from those who have too much to those who have too little — it requires, by its own logic, the continued existence of the condition it claims to solve. The deficit must remain nameable for the transfer to have a target.

**Equity, as currently practised, may structurally depend on the perpetuation of inequity.**

That is not cynicism. It is a design observation. And it is precisely why Horton’s instinct — that something is wrong with equity as the north star — is correct, even if his answer of liberty anterior leaves a prior question unasked.

## **III. The Prior Question**

Horton is right that liberty matters more than equity has been willing to admit. The equity advocates are right that liberty without fairness is a privilege masquerading as a principle. But both arguments share a hidden assumption — one so embedded it becomes invisible.

*They assume the person at the centre of this debate is already positioned to receive either.*

*They assume she can see.*

But what of the person who has lived so long inside structural violence — inside the accumulated weight of poverty, malnutrition, preventable illness, inadequate education — that liberty is not a denied right but an unconceived one? What does agency mean to someone who has never been enabled to imagine themselves as an agent?

***What is an agency to navigate, handed over to the blindfolded?***

The liberty-equity debate is not wrong. It is premature. It is a conversation about the second floor of a building whose foundation has not been poured. In the presence of structural violence and social suffering, equity does not function as a destination — it functions as a transitioning mechanism. A phase designed to remove the blindfold. To position a person to begin conceiving of liberty as something available to them. To feel, perhaps for the first time, capable of dreaming about what self-determination might mean for their one life.

That foundation has a name. It is not liberty. It is not equity. It is **enablement.**

Health systems, education systems, nutrition systems — the infrastructure of human potential — are not instruments in service of liberty or equity. They are the substrate within which both become conceivable. They build the cognitive, physical, and social capacity through which a person graduates — gradually, irreversibly — from object of intervention to author of their own life.

This is not an abstract proposition. It is a design requirement. And it carries a practical implication for every intervention that claims to serve human potential:

**Checkpoint one:** Does it build agency? Does it develop the capacity of the person to understand, choose, and act on their own behalf — not as a recipient of care, but as its eventual author?

**Checkpoint two:** Does it reach everyone? Does it extend that agency-building to those furthest from power, furthest from access, furthest from the rooms where decisions are made about their lives?

In a mature system, one that has genuinely done this work,  something important shifts. Structured liberty efforts do not disappear. They step back. They hand the mallet to the individual agency: to the person who has been enabled, who now possesses the capacity to determine their own path. From that point, liberty becomes less a project of institutions and more a lived condition of individuals. And only then does equity assume its rightful and reduced form: no longer an engine of redistribution, but a safety net for genuine system failures and the protected right of every person to choose wrongly. But we are not there yet. Pretending otherwise, by placing liberty anterior to equity, or equity anterior to liberty, is itself a form of structural violence. It builds the second floor first and calls it architecture.

## **IV. Why Should We Care About Any of This?**

Consider the sheer accumulation of effort this field represents. The doctor who stays past her shift. The researcher who flies to Lusaka to present findings to peers who already know what the data says. The community health worker who returns tomorrow to the household that turned him away today. The negotiator who fights, again, for a budget line that will be cut, again.

Why should the sequencing of liberty and equity — the architecture of enablement, the question of who holds the mallet — matter to any of them? Because the answer determines whether all that effort compounds toward something irreversible or cycles endlessly within a system that needs the problem to justify itself.

Getting the sequence right, i.e., enablement first, then the dual checkpoint of liberty and equity simultaneously, is the difference between a health system that graduates its beneficiaries and one that quietly depends on their continued dependence. Between a helper who helps in order to become unnecessary and one who helps in order to remain needed.

What this entire effort ultimately reveals — centuries of public health, decades of global health architecture, generations of community workers — is neither naivety nor cynicism. Naivety would have exhausted itself long ago against the weight of structural violence. Cynicism would never have boarded the flight. What it reveals is something harder and more durable than both: a species-level optimism. A collective, largely unspoken belief that the gap between the world as it is and the world as it could be is not a fixed condition but a design problem. That better systems are buildable. That the blindfold is removable. That agency, once developed, is irreversible.

**That when human beings are given the infrastructure to be good to each other — the health, the education, the nutrition that develops their fullest agency — they more often than not choose it. That, at least, is the wager this work is built on.**

*Liberty matters. Horton is right about that. The person who cannot determine their own life cannot flourish, regardless of how equitably their suffering is distributed.*

*Equity matters too. The structurally excluded cannot claim a liberty that was never made available to them.*

*But neither can be anterior to the other — because neither can exist without something that precedes both.*

***Before liberty. Before equity. There must be a person who has been enabled to conceive of either.***

*That is the work. That is what health systems, at their most honest, are actually for.*

*— Yonas Gebregiorgis Hagos, MD, MSc*
